rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This passage is the second account in the Quran’s textual order of Adam’s creation, temptation, and banishment; related accounts occur elsewhere.
rows.anchor: The narrative in these verses represents the second account (in the textual order of the Quran) of Adam’s creation, temptation, and banishment;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural address includes all humanity, originally created with Adam as the seed in his loins, so humanity shares the story, Adam’s honor, and its commands and warnings.
rows.anchor: all human beings can be understood as having participated in the events of the narrative that follows

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shared primordial human story is connected with the pretemporal covenant in which all humanity witnessed to God’s Lordship.
rows.anchor: where all human beings bear witness to God’s Lordship in a pretemporal covenant:

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Th
rows.claim: The verse is read as mankind’s creation as a whole through Adam, followed by God’s shaping each individual in the womb or in Adam’s loins.
rows.anchor: then We formed you refers to God’s shaping each individual, in either the womb of the mother or the loins of Adam (Ṭ, Th).

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Another reading takes creation and formation to refer directly to Adam and only representatively to the rest of humanity.
rows.anchor: Others considered these statements to refer directly to God’s creation and formation of Adam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran also describes God creating the first human from clay with His two Hands.
rows.anchor: For God’s having created the first human being from clay with His two Hands, see 38:71–75.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command that angels prostrate to Adam recurs in the Adam accounts and can imply that primordial humanity stood above the angels.
rows.anchor: is a key element in all accounts of Adam’s creation (2:34; 15:29; 17:61; 18:50; 20:116; 38:73–74)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Some commentators treat the prostration as symbolic, or say the angels bowed to God with Adam as their prayer direction.
rows.anchor: they say that the angels were ultimately bowing to God and taking Adam as their qiblah, or direction of prayer (R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prostration can honor another’s spiritual greatness without worship, as in Joseph’s family bowing to him.
rows.anchor: It is also possible to prostrate in recognition of the spiritual greatness of another rather than as a form of worship;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording makes Iblis seem to belong to the angels, supporting that classification, while 18:50 calls him one of the jinn; scholars debate the issue.
rows.anchor: suggests that Iblīs is among the angels, represents an important Quranic basis for the idea that Iblīs was himself an angel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iblis defends his refusal by claiming superiority because he was made from fire and Adam from clay, which he regards as nobler.
rows.anchor: Iblīs explains his refusal to prostrate before Adam by asserting his superiority over Adam on the basis of the argument that he was created from fire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iblis’s fire-versus-clay argument recurs in 38:76 and is implicit in 15:33; his fire-origin also lends support to the view that he was a jinn.
rows.anchor: Iblīs’s claim to have been created from fire lends some support to the view that Iblīs was a jinn

rows.speaker: Q, R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Fire’s luminosity, subtlety, and lightness coexist with fickleness, recklessness, restlessness, and destructiveness, traits that fit Iblis’s arrogance and downfall.
rows.anchor: Although fire may be luminous, subtle, and characterized by levity and lightness (Q, R, Ṭ), it is also associated with fickleness, recklessness, restlessness, and destructiveness

rows.speaker: R, Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Clay is lowly and dark but also stable, humble, and forbearing; these qualities in Adam lead him to seek and receive forgiveness.
rows.anchor: clay or earth is base, heavy, dark, and low lying (R), but also has the properties of gravity, forbearance, humility, and stability.

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Clay can serve as a place of prayer, and its elements, water and earth, purify ritually; fire instead is a means of punishment in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: water and earth—that serve as a means of ritual purification (see 4:43; 5:6), not fire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By focusing only on material origin, Iblis overlooks Adam’s ennoblement through God’s Hands, His Spirit, and exceptional knowledge.
rows.anchor: Iblīs’s argument, based purely on the original substance from which Adam was created, makes Iblīs blind to other ways in which God had ennobled Adam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iblis uses human analogical reasoning, or qiyas, against a direct Divine command; Sunni jurisprudence counts qiyas among its four major legal sources, and logic also uses it.
rows.anchor: is one of the four major sources of law in Sunni schools of Islamic jurisprudence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Hanbali school generally opposes qiyas or uses it only rarely.
rows.anchor: although generally opposed or used only rarely in the Ḥanbalī school

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some cite Iblis’s analogy as a reason to reject qiyas, especially in Jaʿfarī Shiism, with the slogan that Iblis was its first user.
rows.anchor: it is sometimes cited as a reason to discount or reject qiyās as a source of law, notably in the Jaʿfarī Shiite school

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fault was using analogy to oppose or subvert God’s direct command, not analogical reasoning itself; jurists who accept qiyas subordinate it to Quran and Prophetic practice.
rows.anchor: the problem in the case of Iblīs stemmed not from his use of analogical reasoning as such

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iblis’s command to get down from the Garden also appears in 2:36 and 20:123; verse 24 gives Adam and his wife a similar command.
rows.anchor: The command to Iblīs, Get down from it—that is, leave the Garden—is also found in 2:36 and 20:123

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Garden permits no arrogance and instead calls for humility and obedience; some say Iblis’s arrogance, as well as or more than disobedience, caused his exile.
rows.anchor: some have suggested that Iblīs’s arrogance, even more than or in addition to his disobedience, was the cause of his exile from the Garden

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: The verse warns that human arrogance can bar a person from the paradisal Garden.
rows.anchor: since this may bar one from the paradisal Garden (Bḍ).

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: Although banished, Iblis asks and receives reprieve so he will neither die nor be punished until the universal Resurrection and Judgment.
rows.anchor: he asks for, and is granted, respite from God, so that he will neither die nor be punished (Bḍ)

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Some commentators regard Iblis’s claim that God caused him to err as true, though it does not excuse him, and relate it to verses where God lets people go astray.
rows.anchor: some commentators have considered Iblīs’s claim to represent a true statement, albeit one that does not excuse his actions (R, Z)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Another explanation is that God’s command to prostrate exposed Iblis’s concealed pride and stubbornness, thereby causing his error.
rows.anchor: God caused Iblīs to err only insofar as His command to Iblīs to prostrate before Adam uncovered Iblīs’s hidden pride and stubbornness (R).

rows.speaker: Aj and R
rows.claim: Some theologians and mystics imagine that God deliberately commanded Iblis to do what He knew he could not do, creating an impossible dilemma.
rows.anchor: Some even suggested that in commanding Iblīs to prostrate before Adam, God put Iblīs in a deliberately impossible position

rows.speaker: Aj and R
rows.claim: In this imagined dilemma, Iblis could obey God’s command by bowing to Adam only by compromising his obligation to worship God alone.
rows.anchor: prostrating before Adam would mean bowing to someone other than God (see Aj and R for brief references to this idea).

rows.speaker: al-Ḥallāj
rows.claim: Al-Hallaj imagines Iblis as God’s sincere lover, unwilling to bow to anyone but God even at the cost of destruction and eternal banishment.
rows.anchor: al-Ḥallāj (d. 309/922) famously imagined Iblīs as a sincere lover of God who could not bring himself to bow to anyone other than Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Having despaired of mercy and forgiveness, Iblis resolves to destroy humanity’s relationship with God; his name may derive from ablasa, “to despair.”
rows.anchor: became intent on destroying the relationship between God and His newly privileged creature.

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Z suggests Iblis may also blame Adam or humankind for his fall and seek to corrupt them in turn.
rows.anchor: Iblīs also blamed Adam or human beings as a whole for his fall into error

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The straight path means Islam or true religion, so Iblis targets believers who seek to obey God.
rows.anchor: On Thy straight path means on the path of Islam, or true religion (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan misleads by whispering, including to Adam, as well as by commanding indecency.
rows.anchor: “whispering” to them, as he does to Adam (7:20; 20:120); “commanding indecency” (2:268; 24:21)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan deranges people by touch or voice, makes them slip, and sows fear.
rows.anchor: with his touch (2:275) or voice (17:64);

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan makes false promises and incites hostility between people, sometimes through wine and gambling.
rows.anchor: making them (false) promises (4:120; 14:22; 17:64); inciting evil between them (12:100; 17:53)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan makes evil deeds seem fair, causes people to forget God’s commands, and even attempts to alter revelation.
rows.anchor: causing them to forget God and His commandments (6:68; 12:42; 18:63; 58:19); and even by attempting to alter revelation (22:52).

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Razi reads Satan’s approach from front and behind as creating doubts in Resurrection and Judgment or worldly eternity, weakening desire for the Hereafter, or provoking rejection of prophets past and present.
rows.anchor: According to al-Rāzī, that Satan will come upon them from in front of them and from behind them

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Razi interprets the approaches from all four directions as forms of misguidance: front and behind concern judgment, worldly desire, and rejection of prophets; right and left signify disbelief and religious innovation.
rows.anchor: According to al-Rāzī, that Satan will come upon them from in front of them and from behind them

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: In an account of the four directions, angels pity humanity and ask how people can escape; God says supplication upward and humble prostration downward remain open paths to forgiveness.
rows.anchor: al-Rāzī says that when Satan made this vow to mislead human beings, the angels’ hearts softened toward them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iblis’s prediction that most people will be ungrateful proves accurate, though 34:20 exempts a group of believers.
rows.anchor: the Quran elsewhere indicates that Iblīs’s prediction Thou wilt not find most of them thankful is indeed accurate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other passages similarly narrate the Divine response to Iblis’s refusal and defense.
rows.anchor: For similar presentations of the Divine reaction to Iblīs’s refusal to prostrate and his argument defending his refusal, see 15:34–35

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being told to leave the Garden does not necessarily mean Iblis left the celestial realm; his continued presence in Paradise lets him later tempt Adam and Eve.
rows.anchor: he has been banished from the Garden, but not necessarily from the celestial realm altogether—hence Iblīs’s continued presence in Paradise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The order to go forth (ukhruj) differs from the later order to descend (ahbitū), which addresses Iblis, Adam, and his wife together and marks their descent from the celestial realm.
rows.anchor: issued to Iblīs, Adam, and his wife collectively in v. 24

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat implies Satan and the disbelieving, iniquitous people he misleads will be punished in Hell together; other verses say evil humans and jinn share that fate.
rows.anchor: Satan, along with the disbelieving and iniquitous human beings he misleads, will be punished in Hell together.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another perspective says Satan is already in Hell, which in a sense exists now as well as in the future.
rows.anchor: Satan can be said to be already in Hell, which exists, in a sense, even now and not just in the future.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account parallels 2:35. Adam’s wife is Eve, called Ḥawwāʾ in Islamic tradition, though the Quran never names her.
rows.anchor: Eve, or Ḥawwāʾ in Arabic, whose name does not appear in the Quran, although it is commonly used in the Islamic tradition.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eve enters without an account of her origin; although primordial Adam represents all humanity, male and female, the Quran does not explain how this Adam becomes the first couple.
rows.anchor: the Quran does not explicitly discuss the process by which this primordial Adam is differentiated into the first male and female

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Bible’s rib account appears in Hadith; many commentators read 4:1 as an oblique reference to Eve’s creation from Adam, understood here as primordial and androgynic humanity.
rows.anchor: The Biblical story of Eve’s creation from Adam’s rib (Genesis 2:21–22), however, is referenced in the Ḥadīth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam and Eve may eat any Garden fruit except the forbidden tree, variously identified as wheat, fig, or grape and called the Tree of Everlastingness elsewhere; this differs from the Biblical tree of knowledge.
rows.anchor: commentators variously describe as a wheat or grain plant, a fig tree, or a grapevine

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Iblis’s whisper may be a quiet spoken message or a subtle suggestion to the heart, intended to tempt disobedience.
rows.anchor: meaning either that he spoke to them openly in a low voice or that he spoke subtly to their hearts (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan’s whisper exposes nakedness that had been hidden; the Quran and Bible both connect the couple’s disobedience with awareness of nakedness, followed by discussion of clothing.
rows.anchor: thereby to expose . . . their nakedness, which had been hidden from them

rows.speaker: JJ, Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: The nakedness of Adam and Eve is widely understood as their private parts.
rows.anchor: The nakedness of Adam and Eve is widely glossed as a reference to their private parts (JJ, Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: Wahb ibn Munabbih
rows.claim: Wahb ibn Munabbih says Adam and Eve were originally clothed in light, which concealed their private parts.
rows.anchor: according to the early narrator and traditionist Wahb ibn Munabbih (d. early second/eighth century), Adam and Eve were initially cloaked in light

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sawʾah, translated “nakedness,” comes from a root meaning bad or evil; exposing it is described as corrupting.
rows.anchor: Nakedness translates sawʾah, which derives from a root meaning something that is bad or evil

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: R says exposing nakedness, specifically the private parts, corrupts human beings.
rows.anchor: exposing one’s nakedness, or private parts specifically, is corrupting for human beings (R)

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Many commentators treat the verse as evidence that exposing private parts is inherently sinful except in legally permitted contexts such as marriage.
rows.anchor: many commentators see this verse as evidence that exposing one’s private parts (except in legally permitted contexts, such as marriage) is inherently sinful (R, Z).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan falsely claims God forbade the fruit only to keep Adam and Eve from becoming angels or immortal.
rows.anchor: Iblīs tempts Adam and his wife by suggesting falsely that God had forbidden them the fruit of the tree only because eating it would allow them to become angels

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: A minority reading vocalizes malakayn as malikayn, making the promise that the pair could become rulers of a kingdom rather than angels.
rows.anchor:
lest you should become sovereigns of the
kingdom (
malikayn
)” (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By promising angelhood or immortality, Satan raises false hopes and desires, a recurring satanic tactic.
rows.anchor: Satan raises in them false hopes and desires, a satanic tactic mentioned elsewhere

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Th, Z
rows.claim: Commentators say Satan swore by God that he was sincere, although he had declared evil intent and God had warned the pair that he was their enemy.
rows.anchor: according to commentators, swearing by God (Ṭ, Th, Z)—that he is their sincere adviser

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan draws them through delusion and false promises, his primary tactics; he is given no power to compel people or authority over God’s believing servants.
rows.anchor: Delusion and “false promises” are Satan’s primary tactics—he is the Deluder in 31:33; 35:5; and 57:14

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan has no power to compel people and no authority over God’s believing servants.
rows.anchor: he has been given no power to compel human beings, and no authority over those who are believing servants of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eating the tree suddenly makes Adam and Eve aware of their nakedness because disobedience removes their divinely ordered cover or light.
rows.anchor: their act of disobedience had effectively removed the Divinely ordered cover or light

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike Genesis, the Quran has Satan tempt Adam and Eve directly and both succumb together; Eve is not the cause of Adam’s fall.
rows.anchor: in the Quranic account Adam and Eve are both directly tempted by Satan and succumb to his temptation together.

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Th
rows.claim: Some commentators report that Eve was tempted first, likely following the Biblical account, but the Quran equally implicates both in the transgression and its consequences.
rows.anchor: Some commentators do mention reports that Eve had been tempted first (Ṭ, Th)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam and Eve’s ability to disobey God in Paradise shows that they had free will before the fall.
rows.anchor: That Adam and Eve are capable of disobeying God in Paradise indicates that they had free will even before the fall.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their sudden awareness of nakedness signifies lost innocence and alienation from themselves and from the honored station that had received the angels’ prostration.
rows.anchor: Adam and Eve’s sudden awareness of their nakedness suggests their loss of innocence and evokes a profound sense of alienation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Covering themselves with Garden leaves grounds the Quran’s account of God’s gift of clothing to humanity; traditional sources identify the leaves as fig.
rows.anchor: This awareness prompts them to sew together leaves of the Garden to cover themselves, which serves as a scriptural basis for the Divine gift of raiment

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: Most traditional sources identify the leaves as fig leaves, as in the Biblical account.
rows.anchor: The leaves they use are said by most traditional sources to be fig leaves (Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: several commentators
rows.claim: Several commentators say Adam tried to hide from God in shame, as in Genesis.
rows.anchor: several commentators mention that Adam attempted to hide from God out of shame

rows.speaker: Qu
rows.claim: The statement that God called out to Adam and Eve signals distance and alienation, unlike His intimate direct address to Adam earlier.
rows.anchor: it is said that He called out to them, an expression that indicates distance and alienation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam and Eve immediately admit fault and ask forgiveness, modeling repentance after their disobedience.
rows.anchor: Adam and Eve immediately accept blame and seek forgiveness, saying, We have wronged ourselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their admission shows their disobedience harmed only themselves; human action cannot harm God.
rows.anchor: their disobedience has brought harm only to themselves, for human action does not harm God in the least

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They wronged themselves by becoming alienated from their original nature and from God; God does not wrong people, who wrong themselves.
rows.anchor: their disobedience has alienated them from their original nature and from God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam and Eve’s penitence models the attitude appropriate after sin; 4:64 offers a related example of seeking God’s forgiveness.
rows.anchor: The penitent attitude and words of Adam and his wife model the appropriate attitude one should have after one has sinned

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ, Th, Z
rows.claim: Some commentators say Adam defended himself by noting that Satan swore by God, whom Adam could not imagine anyone invoking to lie.
rows.anchor: some commentators report that Adam added in his own defense that Satan had “sworn unto them by God”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iblis argues for his disobedience and seeks reprieve for revenge, displaying pride and despair; Adam accepts guilt and hopes in Divine mercy.
rows.anchor: Satan’s attitude is thus one of pride but also, it would seem, despair of Divine Forgiveness, whereas Adam’s is one of humility and hope in Divine Mercy.

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The command to descend is widely taken to address Adam, Eve and their descendants, as well as Iblis.
rows.anchor: is widely considered to be addressed to Adam and Eve and their future progeny as well as to Iblīs, or Satan (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This descent means banishment from the celestial realm, unlike Iblis’s earlier expulsion from the Garden alone.
rows.anchor: The command is taken to indicate their banishment from the celestial realm altogether and is thus different from God’s earlier command banishing Iblīs from the Garden specifically

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Some Sufis see the fall as providential and merciful: it led Adam and Eve to earthly vicegerency and created the possibility of drawing near to God through distance and exile.
rows.anchor: Some Sufi commentators emphasize the providential and even merciful aspect of the fall of Adam and Eve

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh teaches that disobedience producing humility and need is better than obedience producing might and pride.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh, an eighth-/fourteenth-century Shādhilī Sufi master, said in his book al-Ḥikam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fall lets God manifest forgiveness and lets Adam, and humanity through him, manifest humility, repentance, and return to God, attaining perfection unavailable without the fall.
rows.anchor: the fall affords God the opportunity to manifest His Attribute of Forgiveness and offers Adam, and by extension all human beings, the possibility of manifesting humility and repentance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mustaqarr, rendered “dwelling place,” means a settled or established place; 6:98 discusses the term further.
rows.anchor: Dwelling place translates mustaqarr, meaning a settled or established place;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earthly life’s temporary enjoyment is repeated elsewhere and is contrasted throughout the Quran with the lasting full reward or punishment of the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: The idea that earthly life entails enjoyment for a while is repeated in various ways elsewhere in the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence of earthly life, death, and resurrection reminds people of their ultimate fate.
rows.anchor: a reminder of which is provided by the reference to earthly life, earthly death, and resurrection (being brought forth) in v. 25.
